claim: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep loss is associated with increased consumption of weight-promoting foods.
source: Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep loss is associated with increased consumption of weight-promoting foods.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known association, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is thought to mediate reward anticipation.
source: The prefrontal cortex (PFC) is thought to mediate reward anticipation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about PFC function.

claim: REM sleep loss increased HPF consumption compared to control animals.
source: We found that REM sleep loss increased HPF consumption compared to control animals.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: mPFC inactivation reversed the effect of REM sleep loss on sucrose consumption without affecting fat consumption.
source: However, mPFC inactivation reversed the effect of REM sleep loss on sucrose consumption without affecting fat consumption.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study's experiments, supported by data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: This study provides a causal link between REM sleep, mPFC function and HPF consumption for the first time.
source: Our findings provide, for the first time, a causal link between REM sleep, mPFC function and HPF consumption.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results showing that mPFC inactivation reverses REM sleep loss effects on sucrose consumption.

claim: People who slept less than 6 hr per night were more likely to gain weight over a 1-year period compared to people who slept 7 to 8 hr per night.
source: A study of more than 30,000 participants found that those who slept less than 6 hr per night were more likely to gain weight over a 1-year period compared to people who slept 7 to 8 hr per night (Watanabe et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Watanabe et al., 2010.

claim: Healthy adults obtaining insufficient sleep (5 hr per night) are more likely to consume weight-promoting foods compared to persons who obtain sufficient sleep (9 hr per night).
source: Moreover, when healthy adults obtain insufficient sleep (i.e., 5 hr per night) they are more likely to consume weight-promoting foods compared to persons who obtain sufficient sleep (i.e., 9 hr per night; Markwald et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Markwald et al., 2013.

claim: REM sleep loss in humans over a period of 5 d was inversely associated with hunger ratings and fat consumption.
source: Shechter et al. (2012) found that REM sleep loss in humans, over a period of 5 d, was inversely associated with hunger ratings and fat consumption.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shechter et al., 2012.

claim: Increased intake of weight promoting, highly palatable foods may, over time, lead to adverse health outcomes such as obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.
source: Indeed, increased intake of weight promoting, highly palatable foods may, over time, lead to adverse health outcomes such as obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular diseases.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about the health consequences of poor dietary habits.

claim: Healthy adults subjected to one night of total sleep loss reported an increased desire to consume high-calorie foods compared to non-sleep deprived controls.
source: Healthy adults who were subjected to one night of total sleep loss reported an increased desire to consume high-calorie foods compared to non-sleep deprived controls (Greer et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Greer et al., 2013.

claim: Sleep deprivation decreased activation in the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex, which are thought to mediate reward anticipation and inhibitory control, respectively.
source: In addition, sleep deprivation decreased activation, assessed by fMRI scans, in areas of the brain thought to mediate reward anticipation and inhibitory control, namely the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex, respectively (Greer et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2011; Stuss, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Greer et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2011; Stuss, 2011.

claim: Presentation of HPF to sleep deprived healthy adults was not associated with anterior cingulate activation.
source: For example, presentation of HPF to sleep deprived healthy adults was not associated with anterior cingulate activation (St. Onge et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to St. Onge et al., 2014.

claim: A positive association was found between appetite for HPF and anterior cingulate function.
source: while in other instances a positive association was found between appetite for HPF and anterior cingulate function (Benedict et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Benedict et al., 2012.

claim: Mice exposed to a wire-mesh-grid device (WMGD) over a 72-hr period showed significantly less REM sleep after device introduction compared to baseline.
source: During the dark period, mice exposed to a wire-mesh-grid device (WMGD) in their housing cage (Figure 1A) over a 72-hr period showed significantly less REM sleep after device introduction compared to baseline polygraphic recordings obtained without the device (F3,6 = 23.835, p = 0.001; Figure 1B and C, McEown et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis (F3,6 = 23.835, p = 0.001) and reference to Figure 1A, B, and C, as well as citation to McEown et al., 2016.

claim: There was a 58% REM sleep reduction observed between baseline and the 25–48 hr dark time period.
source: There was a significant REM sleep reduction of 58% observed between baseline and the 25–48 hr dark time period (p = 0.026)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.026).

claim: There was a 56% REM sleep reduction observed between baseline and the 49–72 hr dark time period.
source: and a 56% REM sleep reduction observed between baseline and the 49–72 hr dark time period (p = 0.020).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.020).

claim: A 46% REM sleep reduction was found when comparing the 0–24 hr and 25–48 hr dark time periods.
source: In addition, a 46% REM sleep reduction was found when comparing the 0–24 hr and 25–48 hr dark time periods (p = 0.009).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.009).

claim: No rebound in REM sleep was observed during the first 3 hr of the 25–48 hr light period.
source: Moreover, we did not observe any rebound in REM sleep during the first 3 hr of the 25–48 hr light period (all comparisons p > 0.05; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p > 0.05) and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A 23% increase in wakefulness during the dark period was observed between baseline and the 49–72 hr time period.
source: Specifically, a 23% increase in wakefulness during the dark period was observed between baseline and the 49–72 hr time period (p = 0.042).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.042).

claim: No differences were observed between time periods, during the dark phase, for slow-wave sleep (SWS).
source: No differences were observed between time periods, during the dark phase, for slow-wave sleep (SWS)—also known as non-REM sleep—(F3,6 = 4.605, p = 0.053).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p = 0.053).

claim: Differences between time periods, during the light phase, for wake, REM and SWS were non-significant.
source: In addition, differences between time periods, during the light phase, for wake (F3,6 = 1.608, p = 0.284), REM (F3,6 = 1.103, 0.418) and SWS (F3,6 = 1.434, p = 0.323) were also non-significant.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results for wake (p = 0.284), REM (p = 0.418), and SWS (p = 0.323).

claim: WMGD exposure increased the number of SWS episodes during the light period, lasting 120 to 239 s, by 44% compared to baseline.
source: Specifically, WMGD exposure increased the number of SWS episodes during the light period, lasting 120 to 239 s, by 44% compared to baseline measures taken without the WMGD (t2 = −18.898, p = 0.003).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (t2 = −18.898, p = 0.003).

claim: WMGD exposure decreased the number of REM episodes during the dark period, lasting 60 to 119 s, by 69% compared to baseline.
source: Furthermore, WMGD exposure decreased the number of REM episodes during the dark period, lasting 60 to 119 s, by 69% compared to baseline (t2 = 9.430, p=0.011).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (t2 = 9.430, p = 0.011).

claim: WMGD exposure increased the number of wake episodes during the light period, lasting 30 to 59 s, by 42% compared to baseline.
source: On the other hand, WMGD exposure increased the number of wake episodes during the light period, lasting 30 to 59 s, by 42% compared to baseline (t2 = −4.355, p = 0.049).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (t2 = −4.355, p = 0.049).

claim: The mean duration of SWS, REM sleep and wake episodes was not significantly different after WMGD exposure.
source: The mean duration of SWS, REM sleep and wake episodes was not significantly different after WMGD exposure (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: SWS EEG power density increased by 12% to 14% after exposure to the WMGD during the light period at 2.5 Hz, 22 Hz and 24 Hz compared to baseline.
source: That is, we observed increases in SWS EEG power density, of 12% to 14%, after exposure to the WMGD during the light period at 2.5 Hz (t2 = −51.786, p = 0.000), 22 Hz (t2 = −49.829, p = 0.000) and 24 Hz (t2 = −31.982, p = 0.001) compared to baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance at multiple frequencies.

claim: SWS EEG power density increased by 12% to 14% after WMGD exposure during the dark period at 2.5 Hz, 3 Hz, 10.5 Hz and 11 Hz compared to baseline.
source: We also observed increases in SWS EEG power density, of 12% to 14%, after WMGD exposure during the dark period at 2.5 Hz (t2 = −42.819, p = 0.001), 3 Hz (t2 = −27.978, p = 0.001), 10.5 Hz (t2 = −121.636, p = 0.000) and 11 Hz (t2 = −46.198, p = 0.000) compared to baseline.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance at multiple frequencies.

claim: No significant differences in REM EEG power density were observed during the 25–48 hr light or dark period.
source: On the other hand, we did not observe significant differences in REM EEG power density during the 25–48 hr light or dark period (all comparisons p > 0.05; Figure 2, Panel C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p > 0.05) and reference to Figure 2C.

claim: REM sleep is specifically reduced during the dark period in mice after WMGD exposure for the 25–48 hr time period, or longer.
source: These results suggest that REM sleep is specifically reduced during the dark period in mice after WMGD exposure for the 25–48 hr time period, or longer
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing REM sleep reduction patterns.

claim: The WMGD may be useful to elucidate the role of REM sleep loss on HPF consumption.
source: and thus the WMGD may be useful to elucidate the role of REM sleep loss on HPF consumption.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the potential utility of the WMGD method.

claim: The altered heteromeric GluClαβ channel prevents the firing of action potentials by hyperpolarizing the cell membrane for several days after administration of IVM.
source: The altered heteromeric channel, which is made up of an α-subunit and β-subunit, prevents the firing of action potentials by hyperpolarizing the cell membrane for several days after administration of IVM.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of action of the chemogenetic tool, based on established knowledge of the system.

claim: The chemogenetic system involves a Caenorhabditis elegans glutamate-gated and IVM-gated chloride channel that was mutagenically modified to abolish sensitivity to glutamate while retaining sensitivity to IVM.
source: Therefore, we used a chemogenetic system that involves a Caenorhabditis elegans glutamate-gated and IVM-gated chloride channel that was mutagenically modified to abolish sensitivity to glutamate while retaining sensitivity to IVM (Lerchner et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lerchner et al., 2007.

claim: The virus successfully targeted the mPFC, including the cingulate, prelimbic and infralimbic cortices.
source: The virus successfully targeted the mPFC, for mice used in all experiments, including the cingulate, prelimbic and infralimbic cortices (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: IVM-injected mice had markedly attenuated Fos expression in the mPFC compared to mice injected with propylene glycol.
source: IVM-injected mice had markedly attenuated Fos expression in the mPFC compared to mice injected with propylene glycol, indicating that the GluClαβ successfully inhibited neuronal activity in the mPFC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The GluClαβ successfully inhibited neuronal activity in the mPFC.
source: IVM-injected mice had markedly attenuated Fos expression in the mPFC compared to mice injected with propylene glycol, indicating that the GluClαβ successfully inhibited neuronal activity in the mPFC (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced Fos expression data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SWS, REM and wakefulness amounts were non-significant when comparing the light and dark phases during the 25–48 hr time period for mPFC inactivated mice to the light and dark phases of the baseline day before the IVM injection.
source: SWS, REM and wakefulness amounts were non-significant when comparing the light and dark phases during the 25–48 hr time period for mPFC inactivated mice to the light and dark phases of the baseline day before the IVM injection (Figure 3D; all comparisons p>0.05).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p > 0.05) and reference to Figure 3D.

claim: mPFC inactivation alone did not affect sucrose or fat consumption in mice.
source: We compared non-sleep deprived mPFC inactivated mice to non-sleep deprived control mice and found no difference between these groups in sucrose (propylene glycol injected mice: p = 0.391; saline injected mice: p = 0.350) or fat consumption (propylene glycol injected mice: p = 0.575; saline injected mice: p = 0.434); indicating that mPFC inactivation, alone, did not affect sucrose or fat consumption in mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Panel A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant differences and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Panel A.

claim: REM sleep loss increased sucrose consumption by 27% compared to non-sleep deprived saline injected controls.
source: Moreover, we found that REM sleep loss increased sucrose consumption by 27% compared to non-sleep deprived saline injected controls (p = 0.039)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.039).

claim: REM sleep loss increased sucrose consumption by 35% compared to non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected controls.
source: and 35% compared to non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected controls (p = 0.033).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.033).

claim: mPFC inactivated, REM sleep deprived mice consumed 49% less sucrose compared to REM sleep deprived controls.
source: Specifically, mPFC inactivated, REM sleep deprived mice consumed 49% less sucrose compared to REM sleep deprived controls (p = 0.004).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.004).

claim: Sucrose consumption was non-significant between mPFC inactivated, REM sleep deprived mice and non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected controls.
source: Whereas sucrose consumption was non-significant between mPFC inactivated, REM sleep deprived mice and non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected (p = 0.205)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p = 0.205).

claim: Sucrose consumption was non-significant between mPFC inactivated, REM sleep deprived mice and non-sleep deprived saline injected controls.
source: and saline injected controls (p=0.060).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p = 0.060).

claim: REM sleep loss increased fat consumption by 26% compared to non-sleep deprived saline injected controls.
source: We found that REM sleep loss increased fat consumption by 26% compared to non-sleep deprived saline injected controls (p = 0.001)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.001).

claim: REM sleep loss increased fat consumption by 35% compared to non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected controls.
source: and 35% compared to non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected controls (p = 0.000).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical significance (p = 0.000).

claim: mPFC inhibition paired with REM sleep loss did not affect fat consumption compared to sleep deprived controls.
source: However, mPFC inhibition paired with REM sleep loss did not affect fat consumption compared to sleep deprived controls (p = 0.199).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results (p = 0.199).

claim: Baseline and follow-up weights of mice in the non-sleep deprived saline injected, non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected, REM sleep reduced and mPFC inactivated groups were non-significant.
source: Baseline and follow-up weights of mice in the non-sleep deprived saline injected, non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected, REM sleep reduced and mPFC inactivated groups were non-significant (Baseline: F3,16 = 0.414, p = 0.745; Follow-up: F3,16 = 0.538, p = 0.663).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results for baseline (p = 0.745) and follow-up (p = 0.663).

claim: Body weight did not significantly change between baseline and follow-up time points for any of the experimental groups.
source: In addition, body weight did not significantly change between baseline and follow-up time points for the non-sleep deprived saline injected mice (t8 = 0.468, p = 0.652), non-sleep deprived propylene glycol injected mice (t2 = 0.756, p = 0.529), REM sleep reduced (t3 = 0.157, p = 0.885) or PFC inactivated groups (t3 = 0.001, p = 0.999).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing non-significant results for all groups.

claim: The amounts of sucrose consumed were not associated with baseline body weight.
source: Finally, the amounts of sucrose (r = −0.175, p = 0.400) and fat (r = 0.246, p =0.240) consumed were not associated with baseline body weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Panel B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant results (r = −0.175, p = 0.400) and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Panel B.

claim: The amounts of fat consumed were not associated with baseline body weight.
source: Finally, the amounts of sucrose (r = −0.175, p = 0.400) and fat (r = 0.246, p =0.240) consumed were not associated with baseline body weight (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Panel B).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis showing non-significant results (r = 0.246, p = 0.240) and reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1, Panel B.

claim: The PFC appears to play a role in mediating goal directed behavior toward highly appetitive food stimuli.
source: The PFC appears to play a role in mediating goal directed behavior toward highly appetitive food stimuli.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about PFC function.

claim: Brain circuits responsible for judging the palatability of foods such as taste, texture and smell are mediated by areas of the PFC including the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex.
source: Brain circuits responsible for judging the palatability of foods such as taste, texture and smell are mediated by areas of the PFC including the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex (Rolls, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rolls, 2015.

claim: The anterior cingulate appears to mediate taste for glucose in primates.
source: More specifically, the anterior cingulate appears to mediate taste for glucose in primates as feeding fruit juice (i.e., a high-glucose food) to satiety decreased neuronal firing in the anterior cingulate cortex using single cell recordings, whereas initial juice feeding increased neuronal firing in these animals (Rolls, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rolls, 2008.

claim: Chocolate flavor increases activation in the anterior cingulate cortex in humans.
source: Chocolate flavor also increases activation, as measured by fMRI, in the anterior cingulate cortex in humans (Rolls and McCabe, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rolls and McCabe, 2007.

claim: Obese patients display increased PFC activity in response to high-calorie visual food stimuli, specifically increased activity in the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex.
source: In addition, obese patients display increased PFC activity in response to high-calorie visual food stimuli; specifically, increased activity in the orbitofrontal and anterior cingulate cortex (Stoeckel et al., 2008; Rothemund et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stoeckel et al., 2008 and Rothemund et al., 2007.

claim: Alterations in PFC brain activity may, over time, result in the inability of obese persons to inhibit salient food cues leading to excess high calorie food consumption and weight gain.
source: Alterations in PFC brain activity may, over time, result in the inability of these persons to inhibit salient food cues leading to excess high calorie food consumption and weight gain.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the consequences of altered PFC activity in obese individuals.

claim: The mPFC contains approximately 20% inhibitory GABAergic interneurons and approximately 80% excitatory pyramidal neurons.
source: The mPFC contains heterogeneous neurons that include some inhibitory GABAergic interneurons (approximately 20%) and excitatory pyramidal neurons (approximately 80%; (Riga et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Riga et al., 2014.

claim: mPFC neurons expressing dopamine D1 receptors mediate food consumption.
source: Moreover, mPFC neurons expressing dopamine D1 receptors mediate food consumption (Land et al., 2014)
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Land et al., 2014.

claim: It is currently unknown what role dopamine D1 receptor-expressing neurons may play in controlling highly palatable food consumption in response to REM sleep disruption.
source: however, it is currently unknown what role this neuronal subtype may play in controlling highly palatable food consumption in response to REM sleep disruption.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about a gap in current knowledge.

claim: REM sleep loss in humans enhances the desire to consume food and increases food consumption.
source: For example, REM sleep loss in humans enhances the desire to consume food and increases food consumption (Gonnissen et al., 2013; Shechter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gonnissen et al., 2013 and Shechter et al., 2012.

claim: REM sleep loss in children and adolescents, of 1 hr per night measured over three nights, was associated with a marked increase in the likelihood of these children being overweight.
source: In addition, REM sleep loss in children and adolescents, of 1 hr per night measured over three nights, was associated with a marked increase in the likelihood of these children being overweight (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2008.

claim: Reducing REM sleep over a 25–48 hr period during the dark phase resulted in increased HPF consumption.
source: In agreement with these findings, we observed that reducing REM sleep, over a 25–48 hr period, during the dark phase resulted in increased HPF consumption.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's experimental findings.

claim: REM sleep was not affected during the light phase in the current investigation.
source: On the other hand, it should be noted that, in the current investigation, REM sleep was not effected during the light phase.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results.

claim: The observed reduction in REM sleep was restricted to the dark phase and not during the light phase.
source: It is unknown why our observed reduction in REM sleep was restricted to the dark phase and not during the light phase.
evidence: This is an explicit statement about a limitation or unexplained aspect of the findings.

claim: Sleep pressure is greater during the light phase compared to the dark phase in mice.
source: Indeed, sleep pressure is greater during the light phase compared to the dark phase in mice
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about circadian sleep patterns in mice.

claim: The WMGD was only able to produce REM reduction during the dark phase when sleep pressure was weaker.
source: therefore, it is possible that our device was only able to produce REM reduction during the dark phase when sleep pressure was weaker.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed pattern of REM sleep reduction.

claim: The REM sleep disruption observed in the current investigation did not occur during the first 24 hr after WMGD introduction.
source: In addition, the REM sleep disruption observed in the current investigation did not occur during the first 24 hr after WMGD introduction.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental results.

claim: The sleep reducing effect of the WMGD requires time to build-up and thus produce disturbances in sleep.
source: A plausible explanation is that the sleep reducing effect of our device requires time to build-up and thus produce disturbances in sleep.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the delayed onset of REM sleep reduction.

claim: mPFC inhibition reduced sucrose consumption in REM sleep deprived mice.
source: In conclusion, our results demonstrated that mPFC inhibition reduced sucrose consumption in REM sleep deprived mice.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's main finding.

claim: Increased HPF consumption resulting from REM sleep loss is mediated by mPFC function.
source: Our results clearly indicate that increased HPF consumption, resulting from REM sleep loss, is mediated by mPFC function
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing that mPFC inactivation reverses the effect of REM sleep loss on sucrose consumption.

claim: The study elucidates the role of the mPFC and REM sleep loss in mediating unhealthy dietary behavior, which may lead to adverse health outcomes.
source: thereby providing clear findings that elucidate the role of the mPFC and REM sleep loss in mediating unhealthy dietary behavior, which may lead to adverse health outcomes.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the broader implications of the study's findings.
